items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22C: Safeguards for automated decision-making
items.locator: Art. 22C(1) and 22C(2)(b)-(d); textual amendment note F1
items.why: The duty itself: safeguards must enable the person to make representations, obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, and contest. Applies only to a significant decision based on personal data and based solely on automated processing (defined in Article 22A). Substituted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80(1); fully in force 5 February 2026 (S.I. 2026/82). Article 22D(3) lets the Secretary of State add to the safeguards by regulations.
items.quote: enable the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller in relation to such decisions

items.title: UK GDPR, Articles 12 and 12A: time limits for acting on rights requests
items.locator: Art. 12(3)-(4); Art. 12A(1), (3) and (4); textual amendment notes F4, F5, F20
items.why: Source of the figure. Article 12(3) covers requests 'made under or by virtue of Articles 15 to 22D', so it reaches requests under the Article 22C safeguards. Article 12A(1): one month beginning with the relevant time; 12A(3): two further months for complexity or number of requests; 12A(4): notice of extension within the first month, with reasons. Article 12A has no page of its own on legislation.gov.uk; it is shown on this Section 1 page.
items.quote: extend the applicable time period by two further months

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling: What are the ADM safeguards? (draft guidance for consultation)
items.locator: Sections 'How do we enable people to make representations?', 'What is human intervention?', 'How do we enable people to contest decisions?' and 'What do we do if someone exercises their rights under the ADM provisions?'
items.why: Source of the quotation ('What is human intervention?', second paragraph). Consultation draft dated 31 March 2026; consultation closed 29 May 2026; not final and may change. Says the reviewer needs discretion and authority to alter the decision and access to the original data, that spot checking does not meet the safeguard, that a record of the review should be kept, and that the three routes are usually exercised together and answered within one month.
items.quote: Spot checking an ADM process doesn't meet the requirements of this safeguard.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How do we ensure individual rights in our AI systems?
items.locator: Section 'What steps should we take to fulfil rights related to automated decision-making?'
items.why: Supports 'what good looks like': a simple, user-friendly route with a link to a member of staff who can intervene; a record of whether the person asked for intervention, gave views or contested, and whether the decision changed; analysis of that record and changes to the system where decisions are regularly overturned. Also says accurate systems still reach wrong decisions in individual cases. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; still refers to Article 22. Year not shown on the page; follows earlier reading lists, to confirm.
items.quote: If a system is too complex to explain, it may also be too complex to meaningfully contest

items.title: Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 1: What goes into an explanation?
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute
items.locator: 'Challenging a decision' paragraphs under the rationale, responsibility, data and fairness explanations
items.why: Why explanation comes before challenge: knowing the reasoning lets a person form an argument, and the responsibility explanation tells them who to contact for a human review. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Year not shown on the page read; taken from background knowledge, to confirm.
items.quote: and who to contact for a human review of a decision

items.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (white paper)
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section 3.2.3, box 'Principle: Contestability and redress'; Annex A
items.quote: should be able to contest an AI decision or outcome that is harmful or creates material risk of harm
items.why: The fifth of the government's five principles, and wider than data protection law: it covers affected third parties and outcomes, not only solely automated decisions about a data subject. Non-statutory; regulators are 'expected' to clarify routes. Published under the previous government; date shown is the last update. Already on the list for AI-interaction disclosure, with a different passage.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 22A: Automated processing and significant decisions
items.quote: a decision is based solely on automated processing if there is no meaningful human involvement in the taking of the decision
items.why: Sets the boundary of the legal right to contest: the Article 22C safeguards apply only to significant decisions with no meaningful human involvement. A token human check does not take a decision outside the safeguards. Inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; 'meaningful' is not defined and can be specified by regulations under Article 22D.

items.title: AI Update
items.quote: This would include complaints about AI decisions concerning the provision of, or failure to provide, a financial service.
items.why: For regulated financial firms the contest route already exists: complaint-handling rules (DISP 1), then the Financial Ombudsman Service free of charge. An AI decision is complained about like any other. A statement of approach, not new rules; it still describes Article 22 and predates the 2025 Act. Date from the FCA's publication page.

items.title: Ethics, Transparency and Accountability Framework for Automated Decision-Making
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation, Cabinet Office and Office for Artificial Intelligence
items.locator: Point 5, 'Help users and citizens understand how it impacts them', 'Context' and 'Practical steps'
items.quote: Process owners need to introduce simple ways for the impacted person(s) to request human intervention or challenge a decision.
items.why: Government's standard for its own automated decisions: a simple route, an accountable officer to answer queries, clear guidance on how to challenge, and feedback loops for improvement. Close to the top two levels of this criterion. Guidance for central government only; date shown is the last update.

items.title: Ensuring statistical models command public confidence: learning lessons from the approach to developing models for awarding grades in the UK in 2020
items.locator: Executive summary, findings: 'Quality Assurance'; see also the principle on 'timing and grounds for appeal'
items.quote: There was limited human review of outputs of the models at an individual level prior to results day.
items.why: The statistics regulator's review of the 2020 exam grading. The appeal process 'was expected to address any issues' that review of individual results had not caught; the predictable hard cases were left for students to contest. Its lesson: be clear on the timing and grounds for appeal before decisions go out. A statistical model, not machine learning; the review did not judge legal compliance.

items.title: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry, Report Volume 1 (HC 1119)
items.publisher: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry (Sir Wyn Williams)
items.quote: the Post Office maintained the fiction that its data was always accurate
items.why: The UK's starkest finding on what follows when an organisation will not let system output be challenged: people held to account for losses that were illusory. Horizon was an accounting system, not AI, and made no automated decisions in the data protection sense; cited for the governance lesson only. Volume 1 covers human impact and redress.

items.title: Use of automated decision-making by government: consultation paper
items.locator: Section on 'Merits review rights' (pp. 30-31); Royal Commission recommendation 17.1 quoted in the introduction
items.quote: The Commission considered that the availability of review pathways are vital safeguards in the use of ADM.
items.why: Comparator, and the route to the Robodebt Royal Commission's finding: where automated decision-making is used 'there should be a clear path for those affected by decisions to seek review'. Also notes that harm can be done long before complaint-based review stops it. A consultation paper reporting the Commission; the Commission's own report could not be reached. Australian public sector.

items.title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
items.quote: a designated staff member of the private sector company or public sector institution able to review and correct the decision
items.why: International comparator. Puts the same three elements as the UK safeguards into one sentence: reasons, the chance to make submissions, and a named person with power to correct. Names private companies as well as public bodies. Addressed to states and non-binding.

items.title: OECD AI Principles: Transparency and explainability (Principle 1.3)
items.quote: to provide information that enable those adversely affected by an AI system to challenge its output
items.why: International comparator. Ties contestability to information: the purpose of transparency is to let an affected person challenge the output. Covers any AI output, not only solely automated decisions. The OECD's own page for the principle; the legal instrument itself (OECD/LEGAL/0449) could not be read because its site needs JavaScript, and the page shows no adoption or revision date. A non-binding recommendation to governments, not a rule for firms. Year is that of first adoption, from background knowledge.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: MEASURE 3.3 (table of categories and subcategories for the MEASURE function)
items.quote: Feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes are established
items.why: A free, widely used framework that makes appeals a measured control: the subcategory goes on to require that feedback is 'integrated into AI system evaluation metrics'. Matches the level where learnings feed improvement. Voluntary and US; not a certifiable standard.

items.title: Conceptualising Contestability: Perspectives on Contesting Algorithmic Decisions
items.quote: the ability to contest algorithmic decisions is being recognised as an important safeguard for individuals
items.why: Analysis of submissions on Australia's AI Ethics Framework, the first to make contestability a core principle. Finds that people expect contesting an algorithm to resemble contesting a human decision, and that there is little guidance on what it requires. Qualitative; Australian consultation responses; the arXiv page read shows no publication venue.

items.title: The Flaws of Policies Requiring Human Oversight of Government Algorithms
items.quote: evidence suggests that people are unable to perform the desired oversight functions
items.why: A survey of 41 policies that rely on a human in the loop. Argues that human review often fails in practice and gives false assurance. The caution behind 'human intervention cannot be tokenistic': a reviewer needs time, authority and evidence, and outcomes should be measured. Government algorithms; an argument from existing studies, not a new experiment.

items.title: Contestable AI by Design: Towards a Framework
items.publisher: Alfrink, Keller, Kortuem and Doorn, Minds and Machines 33, 613-639
items.quote: ensuring AI systems are contestable by design: responsive to human intervention throughout the system lifecycle
items.why: Peer-reviewed, open access. Draws from the literature a design framework of features and practices that make a system open to challenge, before and after a decision. Useful for linking the complaints route to the decision system itself. A literature synthesis, not a test of what works.

items.title: The Right to Contest AI
items.publisher: Kaminski and Urban, Columbia Law Review 121(7)
items.quote: This Article establishes four contestation archetypes that should serve as the bases of discussions of contestation
items.why: The fullest legal treatment of an individual right to contest AI decisions, including a close reading of the GDPR's right for a US audience. Sets out how routes differ: rules or standards, procedure or substantive rights. A law review article; US perspective, written on the EU GDPR before the UK's 2025 changes.
